author: gablooge
text:
## Who needs it, and how we know

Every adopter. The README says enforcement is "one rule: a person may see a record if they are a member of its scope". To apply that rule, the adopter's retrieval layer needs two things from Sluiceway: the record (its format is specified in architecture section 6 and is about to be fixed by B05, #5) and the membership of each scope. The second one has no specified wire format today.

Found (all read 2026-09-19):

- `docs/architecture.md` section 7 gives only a Go signature: `SyncMembership(ctx, t, grants []Membership)`. The `Membership` type is not defined anywhere. Section 3.4 says Sluiceway "maps members to person ids through an identity resolver" and "pushes grants and revocations". Nothing says what a person id looks like on the wire, how a revocation is expressed (the parameter is named `grants`), or what the `http` sink sends for membership.
- The record example in section 6 has `author.id: "U0BEN"`, which is a provider user id. Members are planned as person ids from an email join. An adopter cannot tell whether the author of a record and a member of its scope can be compared.
- The README says "Every record carries a scope (...) and that scope's members". The record in section 6 carries the scope only. One of the two texts is wrong, and a stranger cannot tell which.
- Roadmap open decision 4 says the field names are "a public contract once v0.1 ships, so it should settle before M1 finishes". The membership message is half of the same contract, and it is not on the list of open decisions.
- Other vendors publish this half of the contract. Amazon Bedrock documents the identifier ("email as the universal user identifier"), what happens on a mismatch ("ACL matching fails silently") and how fresh memberships are ("as fresh as the last sync"): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-managed-acl.html . Paragon documents three membership questions its API answers (batch-check, list-objects, list-users): https://docs.useparagon.com/managed-sync/overview (read in the first run, 2026-09-19, growth/landscape.md section 2).

Inferred (my reading, medium confidence): the people described in `growth/positioning.md` (a small team that already owns an index) will design their index schema and their query filter from these two formats before they install anything. If the membership format appears only in M4, they design against a guess, and the format may then be shaped by the code that happened to be written and not by what a retrieval layer needs.

## What they cannot do today

They cannot answer, from the documents, the question "what do I store so that I can filter by user at query time?". They can see the record. They cannot see the membership message, the person identifier, or how a revocation arrives.

## The smallest version that would help

A specification, not code. In the same ADR or next to the ADRs that B05 writes for open decisions 3 and 4:

1. The membership message as JSON, with a JSON Schema beside the record schema. At least: tenant, `scope` (the same string as `visibility.scope`), the person, the operation (grant or revoke), and the time the provider state was read.
2. What identifies a person. A proposal to react to: always send the provider's own user id and the source name, and send the resolved email when there is one, so an adopter with their own identity mapping is not forced through email (see the separate issue about email as identity).
3. Whether Sluiceway sends changes only, or can also send a full snapshot of a scope. A sink that lost state, or a new sink, needs a way to get the full membership. Replaying a snapshot must be safe.
4. Ordering: what the adopter should do when a record arrives for a scope before any membership for that scope has arrived. The safe answer is "nobody sees it yet", and the documents should say so.
5. Fix the README sentence or the record example so that both say the same thing about where members travel.

Done looks like: architecture section 6 (or a new 6.1) shows one membership grant and one revocation as JSON; the schema file exists and validates them; the README and the architecture agree; the roadmap's open decisions table lists the membership format and the person identifier.

## Cost and timing

S (a day or two of writing and one schema file). It must be DECIDED before B05 (#5) closes, because B05 turns the format into a public contract and B05 is the next item in the queue. It also shapes B09 (#9, what the `http` and strict `stub` sinks accept), B23 (#23, what the resolver outputs) and B24 (#24, what the diff emits). The code for access sync stays in M4. Only the contract moves forward.

## What happens if we do nothing

B05 fixes half of the contract. The other half is decided implicitly in M4, a few days before the public release, by whatever B24 needs. The strict stub sink, which is the project's guard against a lenient test double (architecture section 10, principle 5), cannot check membership messages until then. Early readers of the architecture document cannot evaluate the central claim, because the part that makes "one rule" enforceable is not written down.
title: growth: write down the membership message and the person identifier together with the record format

author: gablooge
text:
## Who needs it, and how we know

Every adopter who connects Outlook or Microsoft Teams, which is two of the five providers planned for v0.1. The README says "Webhooks first, reconciliation always" and architecture section 10, principle 10, says "Webhooks drop; reconciliation is not optional". The roadmap's M4 and the backlog's B21 and B22 plan reconcilers for ClickUp, Slack and HubSpot only. No issue or document plans one for Outlook or Teams.

Found in Microsoft's documentation (all read 2026-09-19):

- "Reduce missing change notifications and removed subscriptions", https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/change-notifications-lifecycle-events (page updated 2026-04-07):
  - When a subscription needs reauthorization and the app does not act, delivery pauses. "Any notifications about resource changes that happen when the change notification delivery pauses and the time when the app successfully creates the subscription again are lost. In such cases, the app should separately fetch those changes, for example using the delta query."
  - `missed` lifecycle notifications exist for Outlook message, event and contact only. The response Microsoft asks for is: "Perform a full data resync of the resource to identify the changes that weren't delivered as notifications; for example, using the delta query."
  - `subscriptionRemoved` exists for Outlook message, event, contact and Teams chatMessage. After creating the subscription again, "you can sync the resource data to identify any missed change notifications".
  - `reauthorizationRequired` exists for all resources.
  - For Teams chatMessage there is **no** `missed` notification. Nothing tells the app that a Teams notification was dropped.
  - Lifecycle notifications are sent only if the subscription was created with a `lifecycleNotificationUrl`. "You also can't add the lifecycleNotificationUrl property to an existing subscription by updating the subscription." The subscription must be deleted and created again.
- Outlook, "message: delta", https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/message-delta?view=graph-rest-1.0 (updated 2026-06-19): `GET /users/{id}/mailFolders/{id}/messages/delta`. It works per mail folder, not per mailbox. Application permissions: `Mail.ReadBasic.All` (least), `Mail.Read` (higher). It supports `$filter=receivedDateTime ge {value}`, and it reports deletions and moves as `@removed` entries.
- Delta tokens for Outlook do not have a fixed lifetime ("dependent on the size of the internal delta token cache"). An expired token gives a 40X error such as `syncStateNotFound`, and a `410 Gone` means a full synchronization. Replays are possible and the app "must be prepared" for them. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/delta-query-overview (updated 2026-05-14).
- Teams, "channel: getAllMessages", https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/channel-getallmessages?view=graph-rest-1.0 (updated 2026-09-05): `GET /teams/{team-id}/channels/getAllMessages`, application permission `ChannelMessage.Read.All`, `$filter` on a `lastModifiedDateTime` range. The example response includes replies (`replyToId` is set) and the channel of each message (`channelIdentity`).
- Cost for the adopter: "Starting August 25, 2025, the Teams APIs listed in this article are no longer metered, and no billing configuration is required to use these APIs." The `model` parameter "is ignored when supplied". https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/teams-licenses (updated 2026-04-03; the page calls itself deprecated). Before that date `getAllMessages` cost 0.00075 US dollars per message and needed an Azure subscription, which would have been a real cost for an adopter. That obstacle is gone.
- A developer reported mail notifications that stopped for 1 to 1.5 hours with no lifecycle notification, on 2026-03-17: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5825832/bug-issue-microsoft-graph-webhook-subscriptions-in (read in the first run, growth/landscape.md section 6).

Not verified: the page that used to document delta for channel messages (`chatmessage-delta`) now documents delta for a user's chats, and "chatMessage: delta" in the supported resources table links there. I could not confirm that a v1.0 delta function for channel messages is documented today. The proposal below does not need it.

Inferred: a reconciler for both is feasible inside the v0.1 design. Both calls are cursor based, both use application permissions that the providers need anyway for hydration (`Mail.Read`, `ChannelMessage.Read.All`; the second is from general knowledge, not re-read today), and both fit the existing `Reconciler` interface (`ChangesSince(subscription, cursor, limit)`). Replays from delta are harmless because reconciliation goes through the accept path and dedupes on the record id.

## What they cannot do today

Nothing runs today. In the v0.1 plan as written, an Outlook or Teams adopter whose endpoint was down, or whose subscription paused or was removed, has a permanent gap and no tool to fill it. For Teams they would not even be told.

## The smallest version that would help

1. **At subscription creation (B16, B17, B19): always set `lifecycleNotificationUrl`.** Handle the three lifecycle events at the ingress edge: `reauthorizationRequired` leads to a renewal (one `PATCH`, because Microsoft warns against `reauthorize` plus `PATCH` within 10 minutes), `subscriptionRemoved` leads to a new registration and then a reconcile request, `missed` leads to a reconcile request. Lifecycle payloads carry `clientState`, so the same check applies.
2. **Outlook reconciler:** `messages/delta` for the folders that the subscription covers. The honest small version names the folders (for example Inbox and Sent Items), stores one delta link per mailbox and folder as the cursor, treats `syncStateNotFound` and `410` as "start again from a `receivedDateTime` filter at the last known time", and ignores `@removed` until deletions exist (but counts them).
3. **Teams reconciler:** `channels/getAllMessages` per team with `lastModifiedDateTime gt {cursor}`. A plain time cursor, no delta token needed. Because Teams has no `missed` signal, this one runs on a schedule.
4. If M4 has no room, the honest alternative is to change the claim: the README and the provider table say which providers have reconciliation in v0.1 and which do not. Item 1 should still be done, because it cannot be added later without recreating every subscription.

Done looks like: the M4 acceptance line ("a gap created by stopping the webhook is filled by the next reconcile pass, with the overlap dedupe proven by record id") is demonstrated for Outlook and Teams against the fake Graph server; a `missed` and a `subscriptionRemoved` lifecycle payload each produce a reconcile request in a test; the provider table in the README has a "reconcile" column that is true.

## Cost and timing

M in total. Item 1 is S and belongs inside B16 (#16), B17 (#17) and B19 (#19); it must be DECIDED before B16 is built, because a subscription created without the lifecycle address has to be deleted and created again. Items 2 and 3 are S to M each, fit M4 next to B22 (#22), and reuse the Graph client from B16. The backlog already lists Teams as the third thing to cut if the plan slips; if Teams is cut, item 3 goes with it.

## What happens if we do nothing

"Reconciliation always" is true for three of five providers on the day the repository becomes public. The two where it is false are the two where the provider's own documentation says notifications are lost and tells the app to resync. A reader who knows Microsoft Graph will notice, and this project's whole claim is that its statements can be trusted.
title: growth: reconcile Outlook and Teams too, and ask Graph for lifecycle notifications from the first subscription

author: gablooge
text:
This is not legal advice. It reports what Slack's documents say, what they leave unclear, and what the project could write down so that an adopter can decide for themselves.

## Who needs it, and how we know

Every adopter who connects Slack, and the maintainer before B15 and B22 are built. Pages were read through a tool that summarizes, so the maintainer should check the exact words at each link before relying on a quotation.

Found (all read 2026-09-19):

- Slack changelog, 2025-05-29, https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2025/05/29/rate-limit-changes-for-non-marketplace-apps/ : "commercially distributed apps that are not approved for the Slack Marketplace" get `conversations.history` and `conversations.replies` at "15 messages per request at one request per minute". It applied at once to apps created on or after 2025-05-29 and to new installations. "Internal customer-built applications are not impacted by these changes" and keep 50 or more requests per minute and up to 1,000 objects. Slack points affected developers to the Events API and to the Real-time Search API.
- Slack changelog, 2025-06-03, https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2025/06/03/rate-limits-clarity/ : "Any internal customer-built apps will maintain their existing rate limits". The entry does not define "internal customer-built app".
- The method reference today, https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/conversations.history/ : "For new applications and installation commercially distributed outside of the Marketplace, this method is rate limited to 1 request per minute", and the `limit` parameter has a maximum and default of 15. "For Marketplace and internal customer-built applications, this method has Tier 3 rate limits". So the restriction is still documented on 2026-09-19. I found no reversal in Slack's own pages. (Onyx's documentation says Slack "reversed these API restrictions": https://docs.onyx.app/admins/connectors/official/slack/slack_federated , read in the first run. I could not confirm that from Slack.)
- Slack API Terms of Service, effective 2025-10-10, https://slack.com/terms-of-service/api :
  - "By 'Commercially Distribute' we mean any situation where your Application integrates with Slack APIs and users could pay fees for your product, service, or features", including "a free App that connects to a paid product or service".
  - "These restrictions do not apply if your Application and any products or services connected to it were created for use only by a single third party."
  - For the Data Access API and the Real-Time Search API: "you may not create persistent copies, archives, indexes, or long-term data stores of other organizations' API Data."
  - "you may not: (A) use API Data to train a large language model".

Inferred (my reading, not Slack's statement; medium confidence):

1. A company that self-hosts Sluiceway, creates its own Slack app in its own workspace, and uses the data only inside the company looks like an "internal customer-built application". Nobody pays fees for that app, and it is used by one organization. Normal limits should apply.
2. It is unclear whether an app that an adopter creates from a manifest published by an open source project counts as "customer-built". Slack does not define the term. The adopter creates and owns the app, which supports that reading.
3. It is not the same case when a vendor or a consultancy runs Sluiceway to ingest the workspaces of its customers, or when the adopter's assistant is itself a paid product used by other organizations. The definition of "Commercially Distribute" names a free app connected to a paid product. Those adopters should expect the restricted limits outside the Marketplace, and should read the terms themselves.
4. The "persistent copies" sentence is written about two other APIs and about other organizations' data. Sluiceway plans to use the Events API and the history methods on the adopter's own data. The sentence still shows the direction Slack is taking, and the documents should say so plainly.
5. Slack recommends the Events API. "Webhooks first" is therefore the supported path in both cases. What is at risk is reconciliation and backfill, which depend on `conversations.history` and `conversations.replies`.

What the restricted limit means in numbers (arithmetic, assuming the limit is counted per app and workspace, which I did not verify): at most 15 messages per minute, so at most 21,600 messages per day for a whole workspace. A reconcile pass that visits each of 200 channels once needs at least 200 minutes, and threads need more calls. Filling a one-hour gap is possible. A backfill of history is not practical.

## What they cannot do today

Nothing runs today. In the plan as written, an adopter cannot find out which Slack deployment the project supports, and a reconciler written for 50 requests per minute would be throttled continuously if an adopter's app is in the restricted class. Nobody would know why reconciliation never finishes.

## The smallest version that would help

1. **A statement in the Slack setup guide (B28) and one line in the README provider table**: the supported deployment is a company's own Slack app, in its own workspace, for its own use. Link Slack's changelog entry and terms, quote the definitions, and say that anyone distributing a product built on Sluiceway to other organizations must read the terms and may need a Marketplace app. Mention the sentence about training language models, because the audience builds AI systems.
2. **A Slack rate profile in the reconciler (B22)**: a setting with two values, normal and restricted (1 request per minute, page size 15). The limiter honors `Retry-After` on HTTP 429 in both. In the restricted profile a pass orders channels so that the ones with the oldest cursor go first, and reports how far behind it is. This fits principle 7 of architecture section 10: the limiter must refuse what it can never satisfy, and a full backfill under the restricted profile is exactly that.
3. **A stated backfill horizon** for Slack (for example "reconciliation looks back N days at most", configurable), so the cost of a pass is bounded and documented in both profiles.
4. **A health signal**: repeated 429 responses from the history methods are reported by `/v1/subscriptions/health` (B20) with a plain hint that the app may be in the restricted class.

Done looks like: the setup guide has the statement with links and the date it was checked; a test runs a reconcile pass against a fake Slack that enforces 1 request per minute and 15 objects, and the pass makes progress, never sleeps inside a transaction, and reports its lag; the README table says what is supported.

## Cost and timing

S for the documentation, S to M for the rate profile and the test. The supported deployment must be DECIDED before B15 (#15), because it decides what the Slack app manifest and the setup guide say. The rate profile belongs in B22 (#22) and must be decided before B22 is built, because it changes how a pass orders and paces its work. The health signal fits B20 (#20).

## What happens if we do nothing

The first adopter in the restricted class finds out in production, from a reconciler that never catches up, and reports it as a bug in public. A vendor who builds on Sluiceway may break Slack's terms without having been told that the question exists. Both are avoidable with one page of plain text and one setting.
title: growth: say which Slack deployment is supported under Slack's 2025 terms, and make reconciliation survive the restricted rate limit

author: gablooge
text:
## Who needs it, and how we know

Every adopter who uses access sync with more than one provider, or who has guests, aliases, or people whose address changed. The plan (roadmap M4, B23, architecture section 7) is one identity resolver: "email join (normalized, domain-restricted); replaceable".

Found (read 2026-09-19 unless a line says otherwise):

- Amazon Bedrock uses the same design and documents how it fails. "There is no alias resolution or cross-identity-provider mapping." "If emails differ across systems, ACL matching fails silently and the user receives no results from that data source." "If an email address is reassigned to a different person (for example, after an employee departure), you must detect this before passing the identity". https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-managed-acl.html
- Onyx met the Teams cases in production code. Pull request 14840, merged 2026-09-16: "A member row without an email is resolved by user id. A member that cannot be resolved (another tenant's user) is skipped instead of failing the channel." The same pull request fixed two membership errors that matter for B23: a standard channel's readers are the members of its team, and a shared channel has indirect members from the teams it is shared with. It uses Graph's all-members call for every channel type. https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/14840
- Slack gives the email field only to apps with the `users:read.email` scope; `users:read` alone is not enough. https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/users.read.email/ and https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2017-04-narrowing-email-access/ (search summaries of these pages, read 2026-09-19). Slack's user object documentation says that fields may be absent, null or empty depending on the workspace and the kind of user, and names Slack Connect members as an example: https://docs.slack.dev/reference/objects/user-object/ (search summary).

From general knowledge, not re-read today (the maintainer should check): in Microsoft Entra ID a person's `mail` and `userPrincipalName` can differ, a guest's `userPrincipalName` contains `#EXT#`, and one person can have several proxy addresses. ClickUp and HubSpot members may sign in with an address that differs from their company address.

Inferred: the planned resolver is safe in one direction and silent in the other. "An address outside the allowed domains resolves to nobody" (B23) fails closed, which is right. But a member who resolves to nobody disappears without a trace. The adopter then hears "the assistant cannot see my channel" and has nothing to look at. The second risk is the opposite one: an address that was reassigned to a new person gives the new person the old person's access, and nothing in the design detects it.

## What they cannot do today

Nothing runs today. In the plan as written they could not see who failed to resolve and why, could not map people by anything but email, and could not tell a guest from an employee in the membership they receive.

## The smallest version that would help

1. **Membership carries the provider's user id always, and the email when there is one** (this is the person identifier question in the first growth issue about the membership format). An adopter who has their own directory mapping can then ignore the email join.
2. **Unresolved is a reported state, not a silent drop.** Each access sync pass counts, per scope, the members it could not resolve, with a reason from a fixed list: no email from the provider, outside the allowed domains, guest or external, ambiguous (two people with one address). The counts go to a metric and to the pass log. No address and no name goes into a log line.
3. **Document the normalization** in one short paragraph: lower case, surrounding white space removed, and an explicit statement that plus-addresses and aliases are NOT merged (merging is a guess, and the project does not guess reach).
4. **Document the adopter's responsibilities**, in the style of the Bedrock page: consistent addresses across the five tools, and what to do when an address is reassigned (the provider user id changes even when the address does not, which is one more reason for item 1).
5. **State the scopes and permissions that the join needs** in each setup guide, for example `users:read.email` for Slack, so a missing scope is a clear start-up refusal and not an empty join.
6. For B23, add to the Teams member source what the Onyx fix shows: members of a standard channel come from the team, and shared channels have indirect members. Guests and members from another tenant are marked, which also feeds `origin.untrusted` later.

Done looks like: B23's acceptance gains two lines: "a member without an email is reported as unresolved with a reason, and is never granted anything" and "a guest is marked as external in the membership output". The setup guides list the identity scopes. Architecture section 7 says what the resolver outputs for an unresolved member.

## Cost and timing

S to M. Items 1 and 2 must be DECIDED before B23 (#23) is built, and item 1 before B05 (#5) closes if the membership format is specified there. Items 3, 4 and 5 are documentation for B28 (#28). Item 6 is a note for B23 and costs little if it is known before the Teams member source is written.

## What happens if we do nothing

The design stays safe but becomes hard to operate: people who should see content do not, silently, and the adopter cannot find out why. That is the "fails silently" problem that Bedrock documents for its own users. The reassigned address case stays undetected, and it is the one case where the email join gives access to the wrong person.
title: growth: make the email identity join report who it could not resolve, and carry the provider user id

author: gablooge
text:
## Who needs it, and how we know

The person who has to pass a security review before the assistant goes live. `growth/positioning.md` names this as one of the three moments when the pain is felt: "Someone leaves a channel or a team, and the assistant still answers from it the next day."

Found:

- Stale permissions are the most repeated complaint in the sources of the first run (growth/landscape.md section 6, read 2026-09-19). Truto: "From 9 AM Monday to 2 AM Tuesday, that user can still pull highly sensitive finance documents from your RAG pipeline." https://truto.one/blog/how-to-maintain-document-level-rbac-in-enterprise-rag-pipelines/ . Microsoft ISE blog, 2026-04-30: a revoked user "may still see the document's content in the search index or RAG pipeline until the next ingestion run." https://devblogs.microsoft.com/ise/sharepoint-doc-level-access/
- Amazon Bedrock states its window in one sentence: "Group memberships are as fresh as the last sync. Permission changes between syncs are not reflected until the next ingestion job completes." https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-managed-acl.html (read 2026-09-19).
- In this repository (read 2026-09-19): access sync is a sweep "on its own ticker" (architecture section 9). No document gives the interval, a default, or a setting for it. The M4 acceptance says a revocation is produced "exactly" once, and says nothing about how soon.
- Deletions are first in the roadmap's "After v0.1" list, and `op: "delete"` is reserved in the format. No document says what v0.1 does when a provider reports a deletion. Providers do report them: Microsoft's mail delta returns `@removed` entries "when an item is deleted or moved from the folder" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/message-delta?view=graph-rest-1.0 , read 2026-09-19), and Graph subscriptions and the Slack Events API deliver delete events (general knowledge, not re-read today).
- Microsoft Graph offers change notifications for team membership (`/teams/getAllMembers` is listed as a subscription resource at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/teams-licenses , read 2026-09-19, and is no longer metered). Slack has events for a member leaving a channel (general knowledge, not re-read today). So a faster path than polling exists for two providers.

Inferred: the adopters this project wants will ask "how long after I remove someone can they still get answers from that channel?" before anything else. An honest number, even a modest one such as 15 minutes, answers the question. No number reads as "unknown", and "unknown" fails a security review.

## What they cannot do today

Nothing runs today. From the documents, they cannot learn the revocation window that v0.1 will have, whether they can shorten it, or what happens to content that was deleted at the source.

## The smallest version that would help

1. **A named setting for the access sync interval with a stated default**, and one sentence in the README and in architecture section 3.4: "After someone is removed from a scope at the source, Sluiceway sends the revocation within one access sync interval (default N minutes) plus the time a pass takes. Until your sink applies it, that person can still retrieve records of that scope."
2. **A metric for the age of the last successful access sync per provider**, next to the metrics of B25, so the window can be observed and alerted on. A pass that aborts because the provider failed (which is the right behavior) makes the window longer, and the adopter must be able to see that.
3. **A plain statement about deletions in v0.1**: deleted source content stays in the adopter's index until deletions ship, and edits arrive as new versions with `supersedes`. Say what the pipeline does with a delete event in v0.1. A proposal: count it, log it without content, deliver nothing, and never send it to the dead letters, so that the dead letters stay meaningful.
4. Write down, as a candidate for after v0.1, the event-driven path: membership events from Slack and Graph trigger an immediate access sync of the one scope. Do not build it now.

Done looks like: the interval has a name, a default and a line in `sluiceway help`; the README's first screen or its guarantees block states the window; the metric exists with the B25 metrics; the architecture document says what a delete event does in v0.1.

## Cost and timing

S. The interval, the statement and the delete-event behavior must be DECIDED before B24 (#24) is built (the sweep takes its interval from somewhere) and before B15 to B17 (#15, #16, #17) decide what their parsers do with delete events. The metric fits B25 (#25). The README sentence fits B28 (#28). Deletions themselves stay after v0.1, as the roadmap says. This issue does not ask to move them.

## What happens if we do nothing

The project's central promise gets an unstated exception. The first serious evaluator asks for the revocation window, finds no number, and measures it themselves, or stops. Delete events get whatever behavior each provider package happens to give them, and the five may differ.
title: growth: state how fast a removed member loses access, and what v0.1 does with deleted content

author: gablooge
text:
## Who needs it, and how we know

The newcomer at M6, and the adopter who asks "how do I enforce these permissions in MY retrieval layer?".

Found:

- The roadmap's quickstart ends in "a record at the stub sink" (M6), and the compose stack (M5, B27) runs "the M1 acceptance test". A JSON record in a test double proves exactly-once delivery. It does not show the thing the project is named for: two people asking the same question and getting different results.
- Every vendor guide found in the first run answers the enforcement question with a concrete pattern: filter in the index before retrieval, fetch more than needed, filter again, optionally check the source. Truto, 2026-05-06: https://truto.one/blog/how-to-maintain-document-level-rbac-in-enterprise-rag-pipelines/ . Paragon: https://www.useparagon.com/learn/permissions-access-control-for-production-rag-apps/ . Cerbos with a worked LangChain and ChromaDB example: https://www.cerbos.dev/blog/authorization-for-rag-applications-langchain-chromadb-cerbos (all read in the first run, 2026-09-19, growth/landscape.md section 2). Sluiceway has the format and no worked example.
- Which target first. Guides for 2026 found by search agree on the order of adoption: "the right first vector database is the one you already run", which for most teams is Postgres with pgvector; Qdrant is named for filter performance; Elasticsearch and OpenSearch "if you already run them for keyword search". Sources: https://chat2db.ai/resources/blog/vector-database-for-rag and https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/best-vector-databases (search summaries read 2026-09-19; I did not open the pages, and these are vendor blogs, not surveys. Low to medium confidence.)
- Show HN asks for "something you've made that other people can play with": https://news.ycombinator.com/showhn.html (first run, 2026-09-19).

Inferred:

- Postgres is the target that unblocks the most people at the lowest cost, for a reason that is specific to this project: every Sluiceway adopter already runs Postgres 16 or newer, because Sluiceway needs it. A membership join is plain SQL and needs no new service in the demo. The join is the same with or without pgvector, so the example does not need an embedding model.
- Filter-based engines (Qdrant, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch) share one pattern: at query time, look up the scopes the user is a member of, and pass them as a terms filter on `visibility.scope`. One documented pattern with two short snippets covers them. The limit to state honestly: a user in thousands of scopes makes a large filter.
- Authorization engines (OpenFGA, SpiceDB) are a smaller audience. One paragraph that maps a membership grant to a relationship tuple (`user:X member scope:Y`) is enough for v0.1.

## What they cannot do today

Nothing runs today. At v0.1 as planned, they can see a record arrive. They cannot see permissions working, and they have no example to copy into their own retrieval layer.

## The smallest version that would help

1. **A demo on top of the compose stack of B27**, with no third-party account: a small script sends signed fake ClickUp webhooks for two lists with different members (the fake provider of B06 and B12 already exists by then). Records and membership land in the `jsonl` sink or in two plain Postgres tables. A second script, or a single SQL query, asks the same question as two different users and prints two different result sets. Then it removes one user from a list, runs access sync, and shows that the result changes. No embedding model and no language model are needed: a text match is enough to show the rule.
2. **One documentation page, "Enforcing scope membership in your retrieval layer"**, with: the SQL join for Postgres and pgvector; the scope filter pattern for Qdrant and for OpenSearch; the tuple mapping for OpenFGA and SpiceDB; and the adopter's responsibilities (authenticate the user, apply the filter before ranking, fail closed when membership is missing).
3. Do not add a new sink for this. If the maintainer prefers, the pgvector sink that the roadmap lists after v0.1 could be reduced to a plain Postgres sink (records table plus scope members table) and moved forward, but the demo works without it.

Done looks like: from a fresh clone, with only Docker, one command ends in terminal output where user A sees a record and user B does not, and after a revocation user A does not either. The documentation page exists and its SQL is the SQL the demo runs, so it cannot drift.

## Cost and timing

S to M. It follows B24 (#24, membership must exist) and B27 (#27, the compose stack), and it fits inside B28 (#28, the quickstart) as its ending. Nothing has to be decided before other work is built, with one exception: writing the SQL join on paper now is a cheap test of the membership format in the first growth issue, before B05 (#5) fixes the contract.

## What happens if we do nothing

The quickstart proves the part of the claim that is easiest to believe (delivery) and leaves out the part that is the reason to choose this project (permissions). Each adopter writes the join or the filter on their own, and some will get it wrong, for example by filtering after ranking, or by treating missing membership as "visible to all". Those mistakes will be reported as leaks of a system that uses Sluiceway.
title: growth: a demo with no third-party account that ends in two people getting different results, and a page on enforcing scopes in your own index

author: gablooge
text:
## Who needs it, and how we know

Anyone who opens the repository: today the maintainer's invited reviewers, from M6 everyone. This issue comes from following the README as a stranger on a clean checkout of `main` at commit 1f4bf50, on 2026-09-19, with Go 1.26.7 on macOS.

Found, what worked:

- The status paragraph is honest and is on the first screen. It says nothing ingests a webhook yet.
- `make build` worked at the first try and gave one 11 MB binary.
- `./bin/sluiceway help` explains itself well: commands, every variable with values and defaults, exit codes. `sluiceway serve` with no configuration refuses with "SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL: required in production". `sluiceway worker` exits with "not built yet, see docs/backlog.md". `sluiceway migrate bootstrap` prints a well commented script.

Found, every place where I had to guess or read source:

1. The README never says how to build. There is no mention of `make build`, of Go, or of a Go version. I found `build` in the Makefile and the version (1.26) in `go.mod`.
2. The Makefile's default target is `check`. A newcomer who types `make` needs Docker (sqlc runs from an image), `golangci-lint` and a Postgres container through testcontainers. None of that is named in the README.
3. The README does not say which commands do something today. I learned from `cmd/sluiceway/serve.go` that `serve` carries only `/healthz`, and from running it that `worker` is a stub. `help` lists `serve` and `worker` with their final descriptions and does not mark them as not built.
4. Who it is for is not on the first screen. The first sentence describes connectors. The audience (a team that already owns its index and self-hosts) has to be inferred from "What Sluiceway is not", which is further down.
5. Postgres 16 as the minimum is in the backlog log and in the bootstrap script, not in the README.
6. The README says every record carries "that scope's members". The record format in architecture section 6 carries the scope only (see the first growth issue).
7. The words people search for ("permission-aware" is there; "document-level access control", "ACL" and "permission sync" are not) are missing from the first screen. Evidence in growth/landscape.md section 6.

Found, what comparable projects show first (first run, 2026-09-19, growth/landscape.md section 8): OpenFGA shows badges, supported storage versions and a production statement, https://github.com/openfga/openfga ; River shows a CI badge, one sentence, then working code, https://github.com/riverqueue/river ; Amazon Bedrock's ACL page shows a boxed "ACL awareness is not authorization", a failure behavior section and a list of the customer's responsibilities, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-managed-acl.html (re-read 2026-09-19).

## What they cannot do today

Build and try the binary without reading the Makefile and `go.mod`. See at a glance what runs and what does not. Recognize in ten seconds whether the project is for them.

## The smallest version that would help

One README edit, all of it true today:

1. Two sentences before the product sentence that state the problem in the reader's words and name the audience. `growth/positioning.md` has a draft.
2. A "What runs today" list by command, updated when a milestone closes: `version`, `help`, `migrate` and `migrate bootstrap` work; `serve` answers `/healthz` only; `worker` is not built.
3. A "Build from source" block of five lines: Go 1.26 or newer, `make build`, `./bin/sluiceway help`; and that `make` or `make check` also needs Docker and `golangci-lint`. Postgres 16 or newer.
4. A short "What Sluiceway guarantees, and what you must do" block modelled on the Bedrock page: it stamps the scope and syncs membership; you authenticate users and filter at retrieval; it fails closed; and the revocation window (see the growth issue about it).
5. The CI badge and a license badge. While the repository is private the CI badge shows only to people with access, so this can wait for M6. The `ci` workflow exists.
6. Optional and tiny: `sluiceway help` marks commands that are not built yet, from the same source as `errNotBuilt`.

Done looks like: a person who has never seen the project can say, after the first screen, who it is for, what runs today and how to build it, without opening another file.

## Cost and timing

S (an hour or two). It fits any time, and costs least now, because the "what runs today" list is short. Items 1, 4 and 5 overlap with B28 (#28) and B29 (#29, "a final read of the README"): this issue can be closed into B28 if the maintainer prefers to do it once. Nothing else depends on it. `SECURITY.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and governance are left to B28 and to the bizdev community readiness run.

## What happens if we do nothing

Nothing breaks. Invited early readers spend their first minutes on guessing, and the README is rewritten under time pressure on the last day before the release (B29 is one day in the plan).
title: growth: README first screen: who it is for, what runs today, how to build it

milestone: M1 · One provider end to end: ClickUp
text:
`http`, the strict `stub`, `jsonl`; wire name as sink configuration; every record validated against the schema in tests.

## Done when

- [ ] The stub rejects everything the schema rejects plus a repeated id with different content
- [ ] The http sink classifies 401/403 as halt, 5xx and timeouts as retryable, 4xx per-record rejections as dead-letter
